reflexion_entries_to_archive.lesson: The PDR justified deleting scripts/deploy-pages.sh with 'running it risks serving 17-day-old S122 code as production'. Reading the 68-line script before deleting it REFUTED my own stated mechanism: it runs `npm run build` FIRST, so it would have served CURRENT code, not stale code. The real hazard was different and worse — it force-pushes dist/ to gh-pages AND explicitly POSTs repos/.../pages/builds to trigger the LEGACY builder, which flips production off the artifact pipeline onto the branch mechanism, leaving two competing publishers for one site. The right call survived (delete it) but for a materially different reason, and the doc I wrote into LOCKED_DECISIONS would have taught future sessions a false model. LESSON: 'look at the target before deleting' is not just a safety ritual against destroying something valuable — it is how you find out whether your REASON is true. A plausible hazard inferred from a filename plus surrounding evidence (a stale branch, a legacy Pages config) can be confidently wrong in its mechanism while accidentally right in its conclusion, and only the mechanism is what gets written down and reused.

The S125 handoff recorded 'e2e: both hostmigration tests GREEN' and 'OPEN ISSUES: None' — true statements about a LOCAL run, which masked that CI's gating lane had been dead for 3 weekly runs. A job killed by timeout-minutes concludes `cancelled`, NOT `failure`: no failure email fires, `gh run list` renders a row that reads like a benign concurrency cancel, and the runner's SIGKILL pre-empts the reporter flush so no report/trace survives to debug from. Three independent masking layers, all of which look like 'nothing happened'. LESSON: at boot, audit run CONCLUSIONS (`gh run list`), not merely that a workflow exists and isn't visibly red; treat repeated `cancelled` as a red flag. And make overruns self-report by setting the test runner's own global timeout BELOW the job's timeout-minutes so the TOOL lands the kill (flushing artifacts, exiting non-zero) rather than the runner — converting a silent cancel into an honest failure with evidence.

This project had logged 16 consecutive instances of external Council high-sev findings dissolving under exact-mechanics triage, and I opened S126 primed by that pattern. In S126 the pattern BROKE in one direction and held in the other, and the difference is instructive. Grok's R1 CRITICAL — 'the soak lane will not be CI-viable; thresholds tuned on local hardware with a real GPU have never run on a 2-core runner' — was CORRECT: the lane hit its 44m ceiling with 5 threshold failures because CI reaches only ~2200 of the designed ~10k ticks, leaving the per-ktick slope noise-dominated (+2249.6 / +523.2 / -308.6 KB/ktick across attempts of the SAME test). Meanwhile Gemini's CHECK findings were both refuted against disk because it asserted about files it had not been shown (it invented a shared upload step and a .gitignore omission). DISCRIMINATOR: Grok's finding was about an EMPIRICAL UNKNOWN nobody had measured (a genuine gap in the evidence), whereas the dissolving findings are consistently about MECHANISMS that shipped code already determines and that can be checked. LESSON: triage by whether the claim targets an unmeasured unknown or a checkable mechanism — not by the reviewer's track record. A finding pointing at a real gap in your evidence deserves adoption even from a source that is usually wrong, and the correct response to it is to MEASURE (here: ship the lane non-gating so its first run is a measurement that cannot red the build), not to argue.

First diagnosis was 'the 3 failing tests waste 9m of the 15m cap, so raise the cap to 25m' — derived by extrapolating an observed CI pace (13 passes / 5m31s ~= 25.5s per test) across all 30 tests. The full local run refuted it: the suite is 16.8m and 15.2m of that is THREE soak tests (worker-heap 9.3m + render-heap 5.9m), which CI had never even reached because they sat among the 14 that never ran. The extrapolation assumed uniform per-test cost, and the unrun tail held the two most expensive files by a wide margin — so 25m would have failed too. The real defect was the lane's COMPOSITION, not its budget. Confirmed after the fix: CI ran the 25 fast tests in 1.6m, identical to local, meaning the fast tests were never slow at all and the missing ~4.5m in the old run was a heap test partially executing when the SIGKILL hit. LESSON: never extrapolate a per-unit average across a population you know to be heterogeneous, especially when the unmeasured members are precisely the ones that never got to run — measure the distribution, then fix the structure rather than tuning the number.
